title: Dies irae
lead: The Latin hymn of the Requiem Mass that opens with the Vulgate words of Zephaniah 1:15, dies irae, dies illa. It describes the last judgment and has been set to music by many composers. It shows how the church read Zephaniah's day of the LORD as the last day.

sections.h: The hymn and its first line
sections.b: The Dies irae is a Latin poem of the 1200s in rhymed three-line stanzas. It is usually credited to Thomas of Celano, a Franciscan friar and early biographer of Francis of Assisi, but the attribution is uncertain. Its first words come from Jerome's Latin Bible at Zephaniah 1:15, dies irae, dies illa, "a day of wrath, that day." The first stanza runs: Dies irae, dies illa, / solvet saeclum in favilla, / teste David cum Sibylla, "Day of wrath, that day / will melt the world to ashes, / as David bears witness with the Sibyl." David stands for the Psalms; the Sibyl is the pagan prophetess of the Sibylline Oracles, whom many early and medieval Christians read as a witness to the judgment. Its old plainchant melody has been quoted by many composers, among them Berlioz in the last movement of his Symphonie fantastique (1830), Liszt and Rachmaninoff.

The poem weaves texts from both Testaments into its picture of the last day. The trumpet that calls the dead to the throne (tuba mirum spargens sonum) is the trumpet of 1 Corinthians 15:52, 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Matthew 24:31. The written book from which the world is judged (liber scriptus proferetur) is the book of Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12. The singer reminds Jesus that he sat down tired while seeking the lost (quaerens me sedisti lassus, John 4:6), that he forgave "Mary" (the sinful woman of Luke 7:36-50, whom the medieval Western church identified with Mary Magdalene) and heard the thief on the cross (Luke 23:42-43). It asks for a place among the sheep and not the goats, on the judge's right hand (Matthew 25:32-33).
sections.refs: Zephaniah 1:15; 1 Corinthians 15:52; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; Matthew 24:31; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12; John 4:6; Luke 7:36-50; Luke 23:42-43; Matthew 25:31-46

sections.b: Zephaniah's day of the LORD falls first on Judah and Jerusalem (Zephaniah 1:4-13) and on the nations around them (Zephaniah 2:4-15), though it also sweeps across "the whole earth" (Zephaniah 1:18). The hymn reads that day as the last judgment of every soul, a reading the prophet's own words do not state but that the New Testament's language of the day prepares (Acts 2:20; 2 Peter 3:10). The two also share a turn. Zephaniah moves from wrath to "perhaps you will be hidden" (Zephaniah 2:3) and ends in joy (Zephaniah 3:14-17); the hymn moves from terror to a plea for mercy and ends with a prayer for rest for the dead. Zephaniah's own setting and readings are on the page for the day of the LORD.
